subject: Applied Thermodynamics
summary: impulse and reaction principles, velocity triangles, blade efficiency, compounding, degree of reaction and reheat factor in steam turbines; gas turbine expansion; the Pelton wheel, Francis and Kaplan turbines, specific speed, unit quantities, draft tubes and cavitation

solution: Concept: Classify turbines by the energy at inlet and the flow direction through the runner.
In a Pelton wheel all the head is converted to jet kinetic energy in the nozzle (impulse), and the jet strikes the buckets tangentially to the wheel: (A).
Francis: (mixed/inward radial) reaction; Kaplan: axial-flow reaction.
Exam tip: Pelton wheels run in air at atmospheric pressure, so they need no draft tube and no casing pressure seal.

questions.text: The nozzle of a Pelton wheel works under a net head of 600 m with a coefficient of velocity of 0.97. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², the jet velocity (in m/s, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: V = Cv√(2gH).
Exam tip: For maximum efficiency the bucket speed is about 0.46V ≈ 48 m/s here.

questions.text: The modern Francis turbine is best described as
opts: a mixed-flow (inward radial at entry, axial at exit) reaction turbine
questions.ans: (B) a mixed-flow (inward radial at entry, axial at exit) reaction turbine
solution: Concept: Water enters the Francis runner radially inwards from the guide vanes and turns to leave axially into the draft tube.
Part of the head is still pressure head in the runner, so it is a reaction turbine: (B).
It suits medium heads (about 40–300 m) and specific speeds of about 60–300.
Exam tip: Inward flow is self-regulating: if speed rises, the centrifugal head opposes the flow.

questions.text: A hydraulic turbine develops 2000 kW under a net head of 40 m at 500 rpm. Its specific speed N<sub>s</sub> = N√P/H<sup>5/4</sup> (N in rpm, P in kW, H in m) (round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Specific speed is the speed of a geometrically similar turbine that develops 1 kW under 1 m head.
Exam tip: This lies in the Francis range; Ns below about 35 would point to a Pelton wheel.

questions.text: The inlet and outlet velocity triangles of an impulse turbine blade are shown. If the blade is symmetrical (β<sub>1</sub> = β<sub>2</sub>) and friction is neglected (V<sub>r2</sub> = V<sub>r1</sub>), then
opts: the whirl velocity at exit is always zero
the axial thrust on the blades is zero, since V<sub>f1</sub> = V<sub>f2</sub>
the relative velocity increases across the blade
questions.ans: (C) the axial thrust on the blades is zero, since V<sub>f1</sub> = V<sub>f2</sub>
solution: Concept: Axial (flow) components: Vf1 = Vr1 sin β1, Vf2 = Vr2 sin β2.
With V<sub>r2</sub> = V<sub>r1</sub> and β<sub>2</sub> = β<sub>1</sub>, V<sub>f2</sub> = V<sub>f1</sub>.
Axial thrust ∝ ṁ(Vf1 − Vf2) = 0: (C).
Exam tip: The exit whirl is zero only at one particular blade speed; the efficiency is limited to cos²α even then.

questions.text: Steam leaves the nozzle of a single-stage impulse turbine at 500 m/s at 18° to the plane of the wheel. The blade speed is 200 m/s, the blades are symmetrical and friction reduces the relative velocity at exit to 0.9 times that at inlet. The blade efficiency (in %, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: ηb = 2uΔVw/V12, with ΔVw = Vr1 cos β1 + Vr2 cos β2.
V<sub>r2</sub> cos β<sub>2</sub> = 0.9 × 275.53 = 247.98 m/s (β<sub>2</sub> = β<sub>1</sub>)
Exam tip: Without friction the same stage gives 88.17 %: friction costs about 4.4 percentage points.

questions.text: For a single-stage impulse turbine with nozzle angle α and symmetrical frictionless blades, the maximum blade efficiency and the optimum blade-speed ratio u/V<sub>1</sub> are
solution: Concept: ηb = 4ρ(cos α − ρ) with ρ = u/V1 (k = 1, β1 = β2).
dη/dρ = 0 → ρ<sub>opt</sub> = cos α/2
ηmax = 4 (cos α/2)(cos α/2) = cos²α (D)
Exam tip: Option (C) is the 50 % reaction result, which occurs at u/V1 = cos α.

questions.text: A Kaplan turbine runner has a tip diameter of 4 m and a hub diameter of 1.6 m. If the velocity of flow through the runner is 7 m/s, the discharge (in m³/s, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: The flow area of an axial runner is the annulus between hub and tip.
Exam tip: Forgetting the hub gives 87.96 m³/s; GATE often gives the hub as a fraction of the tip diameter.

questions.text: The output of a Pelton wheel is governed (at constant head) mainly by
opts: a spear (needle) valve in the nozzle, with a jet deflector for sudden load rejection
questions.ans: (A) a spear (needle) valve in the nozzle, with a jet deflector for sudden load rejection
solution: Concept: In an impulse turbine the flow is set by the jet area alone.
The spear moves in the nozzle to change the jet area and hence Q: (A).
Closing the spear quickly would cause water hammer, so a deflector first turns the jet away from the buckets.
Exam tip: Francis: wicket gates; Kaplan: wicket gates plus runner-blade pitch (double regulation).

questions.text: A Pelton wheel delivers 2.5 MW of shaft power under a net head of 500 m with a discharge of 0.6 m³/s. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², its overall efficiency (in %, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: ηo = shaft power/water power, water power = ρgQH.
Exam tip: ηo = ηh × ηm (× volumetric efficiency for reaction turbines).

questions.text: In a multi-stage steam turbine the reheat factor is greater than one because
opts: the steam is reheated in the boiler between stages
the friction losses of each stage reheat the steam, and part of this heat is recovered as work in later stages
the blade speed increases from stage to stage
the isentropic enthalpy drop is the same in all stages
questions.ans: (B) the friction losses of each stage reheat the steam, and part of this heat is recovered as work in later stages
solution: Concept: Constant-pressure lines on the h–s chart diverge with increasing entropy.
Friction in a stage raises the entropy at its exit, so the next stage has a slightly larger isentropic drop: (B).
Hence Σ(stage isentropic drops) > overall isentropic drop; RF = Σ/overall ≈ 1.03–1.05.
Exam tip: ηturbine = RF × ηstage, so the turbine is a little more efficient than each stage.

questions.text: In a 50 % reaction (Parsons) stage with symmetrical blading, the steam leaves the fixed blades at 240 m/s at 20° to the plane of the wheel, and the blade speed is 180 m/s. The work done per kg of steam (in kJ/kg, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Symmetric blading: Vr2 = V1 and β2 = α1, so w = u(2V1 cos α − u).
Exam tip: At the optimum u = V1 cos α the exit whirl is zero and w = u².

questions.text: A reaction turbine works under a net head of 25 m. The atmospheric pressure head is 10.3 m of water and the vapour pressure head is 0.3 m. If the critical Thoma cavitation factor is 0.2, the maximum height of the runner exit above the tail-race is
solution: Concept: σ = (Hatm − Hv − Hs)/H; cavitation is avoided while σ ≥ σc.
H<sub>s,max</sub> = H<sub>atm</sub> − H<sub>v</sub> − σ<sub>c</sub>H = 10.3 − 0.3 − 0.2 × 25
Hs,max = 5.0 m (C)
Exam tip: High-specific-speed turbines (Kaplan) have large σc and often must be set below the tail-race.

questions.text: Combustion gases (c<sub>p</sub> = 1.15 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.33) enter a gas turbine at 1100 K and expand through a pressure ratio of 6 with an isentropic efficiency of 85 %. The work output per kg of gas (in kJ/kg, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: w = ηt cp(T1 − T2s), with T2s = T1/rp(γ−1)/γ.
Exam tip: Use the γ and cp given for the hot gas, not the air values (1.4, 1.005).

questions.text: For a hydraulic turbine working at different heads, the unit power P<sub>u</sub> (power under unit head) is
solution: Concept: For a given turbine, V ∝ √H and Q ∝ √H, while N ∝ √H.
P ∝ QH ∝ H3/2, so Pu = P/H3/2 (D).
Similarly N<sub>u</sub> = N/√H and Q<sub>u</sub> = Q/√H.
Exam tip: Use unit quantities to predict the same turbine's speed, flow and power at a new head.
